extraction.name: MATH Dataset
extraction.description: A dataset of 12,500 challenging competition mathematics problems designed to measure mathematical problem-solving ability in machine learning models. Each problem includes a step-by-step solution in LaTeX and natural language, with a final boxed answer. Problems are tagged by difficulty (1-5) and span seven subjects: Prealgebra, Algebra, Number Theory, Counting and Probability, Geometry, Intermediate Algebra, and Precalculus.
extraction.creator: Dan Hendrycks, Collin Burns, Saurav Kadavath, Akul Arora, Steven Basart, Eric Tang, Dawn Song, Jacob Steinhardt
extraction.citeAs: Hendrycks, D., Burns, C., Kadavath, S., Arora, A., Basart, S., Tang, E., Song, D., & Steinhardt, J. (2021). Measuring Mathematical Problem Solving With the MATH Dataset. arXiv:2103.03874.
extraction.rai:dataCollection: Problems were collected from high school math competitions including AMC 10, AMC 12, and AIME, spanning decades. Problems were sourced from aops.com/community/c3158_usa_contests and curated to ensure they require advanced problem-solving techniques beyond standard K-12 tools.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Mathematics competition problems from AMC 10, AMC 12, AIME, and other high school competitions. Problems were collected from aops.com/community/c3158_usa_contests.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: Problems span decades, covering competitions from past years.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Problems were formatted consistently using LaTeX and Asymptote vector graphics language. Final answers were normalized to ensure unique formatting (e.g., simplified fractions, consistent fraction encoding, polynomial ordering).
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Problems were categorized by subject and difficulty (1-5). Step-by-step solutions were written in LaTeX and natural language. Answers were wrapped in \boxed{} for automatic assessment. Formatting rules were applied to ensure equivalence in generated and ground truth answers (e.g., ignoring spaces, treating equivalent fraction encodings as the same).
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Problems include full step-by-step solutions written in LaTeX and natural language, authored by the competition mathematics community. Solutions are designed to teach models how to derive answers and use 'scratch space' for intermediate computations.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: LaTeX for problem and solution formatting, Asymptote for vector graphics encoding.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: Models trained on step-by-step solutions showed improved accuracy compared to training on questions and answers directly. However, models struggled to generate coherent and correct step-by-step solutions at test time, often making logical mistakes.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: LaTeX, Asymptote, Mathematica (for generating AMPS dataset problems and solutions)
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: Dataset and code are available under MIT license at https://github.com/hendrycks/apps. The dataset is intended for research purposes and is not sold commercially. Versioning and updates are managed through the GitHub repository.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is designed to measure mathematical problem-solving ability in machine learning models, which could have implications for educational technology, automated reasoning, and AI safety. The authors emphasize the need for new algorithmic advancements to solve the dataset, highlighting its difficulty for current models.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The dataset consists of competition mathematics problems, which may not represent the full diversity of real-world mathematical problems. The problems are sourced from high school competitions in the United States, which may introduce cultural and educational biases. Additionally, the dataset focuses on advanced problem-solving techniques, which may not be representative of broader mathematical reasoning.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is challenging for current machine learning models, with accuracies ranging from 3.0% to 6.9% for large language models. Accuracy increases slowly with model size, indicating that scaling alone may not solve the problem. The dataset is limited to competition mathematics problems and may not generalize to other domains. Models struggle to generate coherent step-by-step solutions at test time.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: Training, Testing, Validation, Fine Tuning. The dataset is intended for measuring mathematical problem-solving ability in machine learning models and facilitating research in automated reasoning. The authors caution against using the dataset for training models to help students cheat on mathematics exams.
